title: One yoke lightens others (Avot 3:5)
hook: Nechunia: take on the yoke of Torah, and other burdens are lifted
tomorrow: what if there's no one to study with?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lonely hours: awake at night, alone on the road, and the danger of an empty heart. Today, a heart that's too full, and a strange way to lighten it.

Calendar like a game of Tetris. Rehearsal, a paper, a shift, a birthday, three group chats all waiting on an answer. The advice is always the same: drop something. So can taking on more ever make life feel lighter? Rabbi Nechunia ben HaKanah says yes, if it's the right thing. Whoever takes on the yoke of Torah, he says in Avot, has the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly cares taken off him. Whoever throws it off has them laid on.
screen: `A CALENDAR LIKE TETRIS.` → `DROP SOMETHING?` → `TAKE ON A YOKE, LOSE TWO.`

segments.voice: Today's question: how can one more thing make the load lighter? Start with the picture. A yoke is a wooden beam across an animal's shoulders. It doesn't add weight so much as gather it, so the pull goes through one place instead of everywhere at once. Nechunia's answer is that a person carries something either way. Take on Torah, its study and its commandments, and the other loads find their place under it. Throw it off, and the same loads come back unorganized, and heavier. The same picture appears in Jewish prayer. The Mishnah says that saying the Shema is accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. A yoke chosen every morning. Now a neighbor. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light." Shared ground: a chosen yoke that makes the rest lighter, rest found by taking something on. An honest difference: for Nechunia, the yoke is Torah, the teaching and its commandments; in Matthew, Jesus invites people to take on his own yoke and learn from him. Neighbors using the same farm tool, each in their own words.
screen: `A YOKE GATHERS THE WEIGHT.` · `TORAH, OR THE LOADS COME BACK.` · `THE SHEMA: A YOKE CHOSEN DAILY.` · `MATTHEW: MY YOKE IS EASY.` · then, large: `ONE YOKE LIGHTENS OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Name one small commitment that could steady the rest: ten minutes of reading at the same hour, a weekly call to someone older, a meal with no phones. Say the wish to yourself, then the thing most likely to get in its way, then the plan: when that happens, I will… Hold the plan quietly until the sit ends.
One yoke lightens others: Nechunia's saying that the yoke of Torah, taken on freely, lifts the yokes of the world.
Hold onto this: one yoke lightens others, when it's the one you chose. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.quoted: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): shared ground with Christianity, in its own words and source (Matthew 11:29–30, KJV): a chosen yoke that brings rest. Honest difference: Avot's yoke is Torah and its commandments; in Matthew, Jesus invites people to take his yoke and learn from him. Ranks neither; the chat's wrong option names the 'all the same' trap. Please have both a Jewish and a Christian reader confirm the difference is fairly put.
'The yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly cares' renders ol malchut and ol derekh eretz. Confirm.
The yoke image (a beam that gathers the pull) is the writer's plain description of the tool, not a claim from the text.
howItsDone: 'Many Jews say the Shema morning and evening' is a description of standard practice; soften to 'Jews traditionally' if preferred.
